intro: A mode describes frequency, not central position. Data can have several equally frequent modes, and retaining all ties avoids an arbitrary choice based on input order.
task: Return sorted tied modes, their shared frequency, and the number of unique observed values.
requirements: Use exact equality of numeric values. Return {"modes": sorted vector of ALL values with maximal frequency, "frequency": that frequency, "unique": number of distinct values}.
If all values occur once, every observed value is a mode.

Unless a requirement explicitly sets another range, numeric inputs are real and finite with magnitude at most 10000. Booleans are rejected except explicit boolean masks. Vectors have length 1..64 and matrix axes 1..64 unless specified otherwise. Leave inputs unchanged. Raise ValueError for invalid types, bounds, shapes or documented domain conditions.

examples.name: Single mode
examples.output:
{'modes': [2.0], 'frequency': 3, 'unique': 3}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

examples.name: Tied modes
examples.output:
{'modes': [1.0, 3.0], 'frequency': 2, 'unique': 3}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

examples.name: All unique
examples.output:
{'modes': [2.0, 4.0, 8.0], 'frequency': 1, 'unique': 3}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

hints.title: Choose the representation
hints.body: Count occurrences for each distinct value before selecting winners.

hints.title: Build the result
hints.body: Compare every count with the maximum and sort all matching values, rather than choosing only the first.

explanation: A mode describes frequency, not central position. Data can have several equally frequent modes, and retaining all ties avoids an arbitrary choice based on input order.

For continuously measured data, exact repeated values may be uncommon. This exercise deliberately uses exact equality and does not impose bins or tolerances that would change what counts as the same observation.
